claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 begins in a homogenized, high-temperature disordered BCC state.
The range of phases formed during cooling and thermal exposure originates from the kinetic evolution of chemical short-range order within the BCC matrix.
Slow cooling permits diffusion-driven local compositional fluctuations and chemical short-range ordering.
Local compositional fluctuations lower the free energy by forming transient ordered clusters such as B2-type regions.
Transient ordered clusters subsequently stabilize into distinct phases.
Rapid cooling suppresses short-range-order development and retains a predominantly random BCC structure.
Controlled slow cooling followed by annealing at 600–700 °C should promote diffusion and evolution of local order.
The proposed structural mediator is chemical short-range order in locally ordered B2 or similar clusters within the BCC matrix.
The locally ordered clusters act as nucleation sites for stable ordered phases that transform the microstructure.
Slow-cooled and annealed samples will exhibit more measurable chemical short-range order than rapidly quenched samples.
Slow-cooled and annealed samples will contain ordered phases, potentially B2 precipitates, coexisting with the BCC matrix.
Rapidly quenched samples will show minimal short-range order and remain nearly single-phase BCC.
Short-range order or associated microstructural evolution may produce measurable changes in mechanical properties.
The mechanism should not operate when rapid cooling freezes atomic diffusion.
Impurities or surface oxidation can override short-range-order effects by stabilizing phases through extrinsic mechanisms.
Very high thermal exposures may homogenize the alloy and erase early short-range order.
Failure to observe increased short-range order, ordered phases, or distinguishable mechanical properties after slow cooling and annealing relative to quenching would falsify the hypothesis.
